etymology: Dominic de Guzmán (c. 1170–1221), founder of the Order of Preachers; from the Latin dominicus, “of the Lord.”
biblical_def: Dominic de Guzmán was a Spanish priest of the early thirteenth century who founded the Order of Preachers, the Dominicans, devoted to learned preaching and the defense of Catholic doctrine against the Albigensian heresy of southern France. The honorable part of his work the dictionary will name plainly: in an age when many clergy were idle and ignorant, Dominic insisted that the church needed trained, disciplined preachers who could expound and contend for the faith, and his order produced great minds, Thomas Aquinas among them, and labored for the spread of doctrine and learning. Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God; an order built to preach answered a real lack. Yet the dictionary cannot honor Dominic as a faithful witness without naming the corruptions bound up in his work and his order. The crusade against the Albigenses, however genuinely the Cathar heresy needed answering, was prosecuted by the sword and folded into the machinery of the medieval Inquisition that the Dominicans came to staff. And the rosary devotion long ascribed to Dominic enshrines the Marian piety that corrupts the one mediation of Christ. Dominic’s zeal for preaching and doctrine the dictionary honors; the inquisitorial sword and the Marian devotion it names as the corruptions of the medieval church the Reformation called the church away from.
webster_summary: Founder of the Dominican Order of Preachers (c. 1170–1221); honored for his zeal for trained preaching, named for the inquisitorial sword and Marian devotion of his tradition.

corruption_summary: The Dominican zeal for preaching is honored, but the inquisitorial sword against heresy and the Marian rosary devotion are corruptions of the gospel the Reformation recovered.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is not Dominic’s call to preach but the means and the piety his order carried. The crusade and inquisition against the Albigenses answered heresy with the magistrate’s sword wielded by the church, confusing the two kingdoms and persecuting conscience—the very abuse the Reformers and the Baptist confessions would later renounce. And the rosary, long tied to Dominic’s name, directs prayer to Mary as a mediatrix and intercessor, corrupting the one mediation of the man Christ Jesus, who alone stands between God and men. Devotion to the saints and to the Virgin, however sincere, robs Christ of His sole office.

The principle to recover is preaching that contends for the faith by the Word and not by the sword, and prayer offered through the one Mediator alone. Faith comes by hearing the word of God; heresy is answered by sound doctrine, not by the inquisitor’s fire. And there is one God and one Mediator; to Him alone the church prays, casting down every devotion that would set another intercessor beside the Son.

etymology: The Western church of the Middle Ages, roughly the sixth to the sixteenth centuries; medieval from the Latin medium aevum, “the middle age.”
biblical_def: The medieval church is the Western Christendom of the long thousand years between the fall of Rome and the dawn of the Reformation, and the dictionary reads it with both honor and lament. Christ promised that the gates of hell would not prevail against His church, and they did not: through the dark centuries the church preserved the Scriptures, copied and guarded the text, confessed the Trinitarian and Christological orthodoxy of the great councils, kept the creeds, baptized, and carried the gospel to the pagan nations of Europe. The monasteries safeguarded learning; faithful preachers and forerunners—Bernard’s hymns, the Waldenses, Wycliffe, Hus—kept a witness to grace alive. The just shall live by faith was never wholly lost. Yet the same centuries saw the accumulation of grievous corruption: the rise of the papal monarchy claiming universal supremacy; the doctrine of merit, purgatory, and indulgences that obscured the free grace of God; transubstantiation and the sacrifice of the mass; the cult of the saints and the Virgin; and the binding of the conscience by the traditions of men above the Word. The dictionary honors what the medieval church preserved and names what it corrupted, and reads the Reformation not as a schism but as the recovery of the gospel the medieval church had buried under the traditions of men.
webster_summary: Western Christendom from roughly the sixth to sixteenth centuries; honored for preserving Scripture and orthodoxy, named for the corruptions the Reformation recovered the church from.
webster_full: MEDIEVAL CHURCH, Western Christendom from roughly the 6th to 16th centuries.

Accumulated the papal monarchy, merit, purgatory, indulgences, and the mass.
The Reformation recovered the gospel the medieval church had buried.

corruption_summary: The medieval church preserved much, yet buried the free grace of God under the papal monarchy, merit, purgatory, indulgences, the mass, and the cult of the saints; the Reformation was recovery, not schism.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name is the long accumulation of error that overlaid the medieval church: the papal claim to universal supremacy over the church of Christ; the treasury of merit, purgatory, and the sale of indulgences that made the free grace of God a transaction; transubstantiation and the repeated sacrifice of the mass set against the one finished offering of Christ; and the cult of the saints and the Virgin that intruded other mediators beside the Son. The traditions of men were bound on the conscience above the Word, until the plain gospel—the just shall live by faith—was hidden from the people. The church had, in the words of the Lord to Ephesus, left her first love.

The principle to recover is the gospel itself, that the Reformation did not invent but uncovered. Christ builds His church and hell cannot prevail; the church that preserved the Scriptures also produced the men who would read them anew and call her back to grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, Scripture alone. The Reformation was no novelty and no schism but the recovery of what the medieval church had buried under the tradition of men.

etymology: The philosophy of the Christian Middle Ages, chiefly scholasticism; from medium aevum and the Greek philosophia, “love of wisdom.”
biblical_def: Medieval philosophy is chiefly the scholasticism of the Christian Middle Ages—the disciplined effort, in the cathedral schools and the rising universities, to set out the faith with logical rigor and to wed Christian theology to the recovered philosophy of the ancients, above all Aristotle. At its best, in Anselm’s “faith seeking understanding” and in the vast architecture of Thomas Aquinas, scholasticism sharpened the church’s thought, defended the coherence of revealed truth, and gave the later Reformed scholastics tools they would put to better use. The dictionary grants the genuine gifts: precise distinctions, the defense of the rationality of faith, and the recognition that all truth is God’s truth. Yet the dictionary marks the besetting danger of the whole enterprise, which the apostle named before it arose: to be spoiled through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, and not after Christ. Where the natural reason of Aristotle is allowed to govern the reading of Scripture, where a natural theology is built that does not begin and end in the fear of the LORD, where the treasures of wisdom hidden in Christ are sought instead in the syllogisms of the philosophers, the servant becomes the master. The dictionary honors the rigor of the schools while insisting that Scripture, not philosophy, is the rule, and that the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the LORD.
webster_summary: The scholasticism of the Christian Middle Ages, wedding theology to Aristotle; honored for its rigor, warned where natural reason governs the reading of Scripture.
webster_full: MEDIEVAL PHILOSOPHY, chiefly the scholasticism of the Christian Middle Ages.
Sought to set out the faith with logical rigor, wedding theology to Aristotle.
At its best in Anselm’s “faith seeking understanding” and Aquinas’s synthesis.
Danger: to be spoiled through philosophy after the tradition of men (Col 2:8).
Scripture, not philosophy, is the rule; the fear of the LORD the beginning of wisdom.

Col 2:3

corruption_summary: Scholasticism’s rigor is honored, but where Aristotle’s natural reason governs the reading of Scripture and the fear of the LORD is not the beginning, philosophy becomes the master it was meant to serve.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is older than postmodernism: the inversion by which philosophy, given to serve theology, comes to govern it. Where the natural reason of the ancients is allowed to set the terms in which revelation must be read, where a natural theology is reared that does not rest on the fear of the LORD, and where the treasures of wisdom and knowledge that are hid in Christ are sought instead in the disputations of the schoolmen, the church is spoiled through philosophy after the tradition of men. The apostle’s warning is not against thinking but against thinking that is not captive to Christ.

The principle to recover is the rightful order of Scripture over philosophy and faith over speculation. All truth is God’s truth, and the rigor of the schools may serve the church; but the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, and God has made foolish the wisdom of this world. Reason is a good servant and a ruinous master; the Reformed scholastics learned to wield the tools of the schools under the authority of the Word, and that is the pattern to keep.
roots_summary: Scholasticism of the Christian Middle Ages; rigorous, Aristotle-wedded; honored for precision, warned where reason governs Scripture.

etymology: A member of the Order of Our Lady of Mount Carmel, founded in the late twelfth century; from Mount Carmel, the hill of Elijah’s contest with Baal.
biblical_def: The Carmelites are a Roman Catholic order of contemplatives, taking their name from Mount Carmel where Elijah confronted the prophets of Baal, and best known through the sixteenth-century reformers Teresa of Ávila and John of the Cross, who shaped the order’s tradition of mystical prayer. The dictionary will honor what the historical record honors: a seriousness about prayer and the inner life, a longing after God, and in Teresa and John a genuine instinct that the soul is made for communion with its Maker and that the Christian life is a pilgrimage toward Him. Where they call the soul away from the world to seek the Lord, there is something the busy modern church has lost. Yet the dictionary cannot commend the Carmelite mystical theology as a sound path to God. Its ladder of ascent toward an experiential union with the divine—the “interior castle,” the “dark night of the soul,” the reach for a wordless absorption—tends to ground assurance and access in extraordinary inward experience rather than in the finished work of Christ received by faith and the sufficient written Word. And the order’s Marian devotion, the brown scapular and its promises, corrupts the one mediation of Christ. The dictionary honors the Carmelite hunger for God while answering that the way to the Father is Christ alone, known through His Word, not the mystic’s ascent.
webster_summary: Roman Catholic contemplative order (Teresa of Ávila, John of the Cross); honored for its hunger after God, corrected for a mystical ascent and Marian devotion that displace Christ and the Word.

corruption_summary: The Carmelite hunger after God is honored, but its mystical ladder grounds access to God in inward experience over Christ and the Word, and its Marian devotion corrupts His sole mediation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the mystical theology itself: a graded ascent of the soul toward an experiential, often wordless union with the divine, in which assurance and access come to rest on extraordinary inward states—raptures, the dark night, the interior castle—rather than on Christ’s finished work received by faith and the all-sufficient Word. The apostle warns against being beguiled through a voluntary humility and the intruding into things not seen, vainly puffed up by a fleshly mind. Added to this is the Marian devotion of the scapular, which sets the Virgin as intercessor beside the one Mediator.

The principle to recover is that eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He has sent, and that the believer’s life is already hid with Christ in God. Communion with God is real, but it comes through the Word and the Spirit applying the finished work of Christ, not through a mystic ladder of ascent. There is one Mediator; the soul that hungers after God is fed at His table through His Word, not led into the trackless dark.

etymology: The rigorist wing of the Franciscan order in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries; from Francis of Assisi and the Latin spiritualis.
biblical_def: The Spiritual Franciscans were the rigorist party within the Franciscan order who, in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, insisted on the strictest observance of Francis’s rule of absolute poverty against the laxer Conventual majority, and who came to be entangled with the apocalyptic prophecies of Joachim of Fiore. The dictionary grants what is honorable: a protest against the wealth and worldliness of the church, a desire to follow Christ in plainness and contentment, and a witness against the corruption of a hierarchy grown rich. Scripture does commend contentment—having food and raiment, let us be therewith content—and warns that no man can serve God and mammon. Yet the movement fell into two errors the dictionary must name. First, it made a particular form of poverty into a gospel, binding the conscience to an absolute renunciation Scripture nowhere commands and turning a counsel into a law. Second, and gravely, the radical wing embraced Joachim’s scheme of three ages of history—the age of the Father, the Son, and a coming age of the Spirit—a false prophecy that set a new revelation above the closed canon and was rightly condemned by the church. The dictionary honors the protest against worldly wealth while answering that the gospel is not poverty and that no prophecy of Scripture is of any private interpretation; the canon is closed, and no third age is coming.
webster_summary: The rigorist Franciscan party insisting on absolute poverty and entangled with Joachite apocalypticism; honored for protesting church wealth, corrected for making poverty a gospel and adding false prophecy.

corruption_summary: Their protest against church wealth is honored, but they made a particular poverty a gospel and embraced Joachim’s false prophecy of a coming age of the Spirit above the closed canon.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is twofold. First, the binding of an absolute, particular poverty upon the conscience as though it were the gospel, turning a possible counsel into a required law and making the form of one’s holding of goods the measure of one’s holiness—when Scripture commands contentment, not destitution, and warns only against the service of mammon. Second, and far graver, the embrace of Joachim of Fiore’s apocalyptic scheme of three ages, climaxing in a coming age of the Spirit that would supersede the age of the Son—a false prophecy that set new revelation above the closed canon and was condemned by the church.

The principle to recover is contentment under the sufficiency of Christ and the finality of the closed canon. Having food and raiment, the believer is to be content; the gospel is not poverty but Christ. And no prophecy of Scripture is of any private interpretation; God has spoken finally in His Son, and the man who adds to the words of the prophecy invites the plagues written therein. There is no third age to await; the church lives by the Word once delivered.

etymology: The Great Lavra of Saint Sabbas, a monastery in the Kidron valley of the Judean desert, founded A.D. 483; Mar, Aramaic/Syriac “lord, saint.”
biblical_def: Mar Saba is the ancient monastery of Saint Sabbas, clinging to the cliffs of the Kidron gorge in the Judean wilderness southeast of Jerusalem, founded in A.D. 483 and inhabited by monks to this day—one of the oldest continuously occupied monasteries in the world. The dictionary treats it as a place of historical and biblical interest. The Judean desert in which it stands is the very wilderness of Scripture: the dry and thirsty land where David thirsted after God, the solitary place that Isaiah said would rejoice and blossom as the rose, the wilderness into which the Spirit led the Lord Jesus to be tempted of the devil. Mar Saba’s chief importance for the church’s memory is as a place where, through long centuries, monks copied and preserved manuscripts and where John of Damascus, the great defender and systematizer of Eastern theology, lived and wrote in the eighth century. The dictionary records Mar Saba’s service in preserving the written Word and ancient texts, while remembering that monastic withdrawal, whatever its discipline, is not the New Testament pattern of the Christian life, which is lived in the church and the world as salt and light. The wilderness is a place of testing and of seeking God, not a higher tier of holiness; the believer’s sanctification is wrought in the ordinary callings of life under the Word.
webster_summary: Ancient monastery of Saint Sabbas (A.D. 483) in the Judean desert; noted for preserving manuscripts and as the home of John of Damascus, set in the wilderness of Scripture.

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though monastic withdrawal must not be mistaken for a higher tier of holiness above the ordinary Christian life in the church and world.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to weigh is the place of monasticism. The dictionary honors Mar Saba’s long service in copying and preserving the Scriptures and the ancient texts, and the seriousness of men who sought God in the desert where David thirsted after Him. Yet it must not be granted that the cloister is a higher and holier mode of Christian life than the ordinary callings of the believer in the church and the world. The New Testament knows no two tiers of Christians; every believer is called to be salt and light where God has placed him.

The principle to recover is the sanctification of the whole life under the Word. The wilderness in Scripture is a place of seeking God and of testing, not a ladder above the common Christian walk; the Lord Himself was led into it to be tempted and returned to His public ministry. The believer hides God’s Word in his heart wherever he is, and the desert’s lesson—the thirst of the soul after the living God—is to be carried back into the streets and the home, not left behind the monastery wall.

etymology: The pursuit of direct, experiential union with the divine; from the Greek mystikos, “hidden, secret,” through the mystery religions.
biblical_def: Mysticism is the pursuit of a direct, immediate, experiential union with God apart from or above the ordinary means He has appointed—a wordless absorption, an inner light, a private illumination sought as the highest knowledge of the divine. The dictionary distinguishes carefully. There is a true and biblical communion with God, a real fellowship of the believer with the Father and the Son by the Spirit, a knowing of God that is warm, experimental, and personal; the Reformed and Puritan writers were rich in it. But this true communion comes through the appointed means—the Word read and preached, the sacraments, prayer—and rests upon the finished work of Christ received by faith, not upon extraordinary inward experiences that bypass the Scripture. Mysticism, properly so called, goes wrong precisely here: it seeks God by an ascent of the soul into experiences beyond the Word, grounds assurance in raptures and visions and feelings rather than in Christ and His promises, and so makes the inner light a rival to the written Word. The apostle warns against being beguiled by those who intrude into things they have not seen, vainly puffed up by a fleshly mind. The dictionary affirms the believer’s true communion with God through Word and Spirit, and names the mystical reach for unmediated union, grounded in experience over Scripture, as a corruption of it.
webster_summary: The pursuit of direct, experiential union with God above the appointed means; distinguished from true biblical communion, which comes through the Word and rests on Christ, not on inner experience.
webster_full: MYSTICISM, the pursuit of immediate, experiential union with the divine.

corruption_summary: Mysticism seeks God by an ascent above the Word, grounding assurance in inner experience; true communion with God comes through the appointed means and rests on Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the mystical impulse in all its forms, ancient and modern: the seeking of God by an inner ascent into experiences beyond the Word, the grounding of assurance and access in visions, raptures, and feelings rather than in the finished work of Christ, and the elevation of the inner light to a place beside or above the written Scripture. The apostle warns of those puffed up by a fleshly mind who intrude into things not seen; the secret things belong to the LORD, but the things revealed—His Word—belong to us. The age that prizes spiritual experience over revealed truth is fertile soil for this old error.

The principle to recover is communion with God through the appointed means and resting on Christ. The believer truly knows and enjoys God—the Puritans called it experimental religion—but the knowing comes by the Word, the sacraments, and prayer, and the assurance rests on the promises of God in Christ. We have a more sure word of prophecy than any vision; to it we do well to take heed as to a light shining in a dark place. The Word is the light; the inner experience that despises it is darkness.

etymology: The family of non-Chalcedonian Eastern churches—Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopian, Syriac, and Indian; oriental from the Latin oriens, “the east.”
biblical_def: Oriental Orthodoxy is the family of ancient Eastern churches—Coptic, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean, Syriac, and the Malankara church of India—that did not receive the Council of Chalcedon (A.D. 451) and so stand apart both from Rome and from the Eastern (Byzantine) Orthodox communion. The dictionary honors much that these churches have preserved: the Trinitarian orthodoxy of Nicea, a heroic endurance of persecution across fifteen centuries under Islam and other powers, an ancient liturgical and devotional life, and, in the Ethiopian church, a remarkable preservation of Scripture and ancient practice. Their survival is a testimony to Christ’s keeping of His church in hard places. Yet the dictionary must name the Christological division at the root of their separation. Chalcedon confessed that the one Person of Christ exists in two natures, divine and human, united without confusion, change, division, or separation; the Oriental churches, following Cyril’s language and rejecting what they took to be the Nestorian tendency of Chalcedon, confessed instead one incarnate nature of the Word (miaphysitism). Modern dialogues have argued the difference is largely verbal, yet the dictionary holds the Chalcedonian Definition as the necessary safeguard of the gospel: the Word was made flesh, full and true God and full and true man in one Person, for only so could He both bear our nature and accomplish our salvation. Oriental Orthodoxy’s endurance is honored; its non-reception of Chalcedon is named as the departure it is.

corruption_summary: The non-Chalcedonian churches’ endurance and Trinitarian orthodoxy are honored, but their rejection of Chalcedon’s two-natures confession is the Christological departure the dictionary names.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to name is the Christological one. The Council of Chalcedon confessed that the one Person of the Son subsists in two natures, divine and human, united without confusion, change, division, or separation—the guard against both confusing the natures and dividing the Person. The Oriental churches, in zeal against the Nestorian dividing of Christ and following Cyril’s phrase, confessed one incarnate nature of the Word, and so did not receive Chalcedon. Whether the difference is wholly substantive or partly verbal has been long disputed; the dictionary holds the Chalcedonian Definition as the church’s settled and necessary confession.

The principle to recover and keep is the full Chalcedonian Christ. The Word was made flesh, the fulness of the Godhead dwelling bodily, taking the form of a servant—true God and true man in one Person. Only such a Mediator could be touched with the feeling of our infirmities and yet offer a sacrifice of infinite worth. The two natures, unconfused and undivided, are not scholastic refinement but the ground of salvation; to lose the clarity of Chalcedon is to imperil the gospel it guards.

etymology: The philosophy of René Descartes (1596–1650); from Cartesius, the Latin form of his name.
biblical_def: Cartesianism is the philosophy that descends from René Descartes, the seventeenth-century French thinker who sought to rebuild all knowledge on a foundation of indubitable certainty, beginning by doubting everything that could be doubted until he reached the one thing he thought could not—cogito, ergo sum, “I think, therefore I am.” From the thinking self as the first certainty, Descartes proceeded to reason his way outward to God and the world. The dictionary recognizes Descartes’ brilliance and grants that he intended to defend, not destroy, belief in God. Yet Cartesianism set loose a method that has shaped the modern mind for the worse: it made the autonomous human reason, the doubting self, the foundation and judge of all knowledge, including the knowledge of God. Where Scripture begins with God—in the beginning God; the fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge—Descartes begins with the self and reaches God only as a conclusion the self certifies. This inversion enthrones man’s mind as the measure and makes the Creator answerable to the bar of the creature’s reason. The Christian does not establish God by doubting; he knows God because God has spoken, and reasons from that revelation, leaning not unto his own understanding. The dictionary names Cartesian autonomy as a corruption of the right order of knowing, in which the fear of the LORD, not the doubting self, is the beginning.
webster_summary: The philosophy of Descartes founding knowledge on the doubting self (“I think, therefore I am”); named as the enthroning of autonomous reason against the biblical order that begins with God.

corruption_summary: Cartesianism founds knowledge on the autonomous doubting self and reaches God only as a conclusion; the biblical order begins with God and reasons from His revelation.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the autonomy at the root of the Cartesian method: the making of the doubting human self the first certainty and the foundation of all knowledge, so that even God is reached only as a conclusion the mind certifies. This inverts the order Scripture lays down. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge; in the beginning, God. To begin with the self and to make the Creator answerable to the bar of the creature’s reason is to enthrone man as the measure of all things—the very posture the apostle warns against, lest any be spoiled through philosophy after the rudiments of the world.

The principle to recover is the right order of knowing: God first, His revelation the foundation, the creature’s reason a servant under it. The Christian does not establish God by an act of doubt; he knows God because God has spoken, and he leans not unto his own understanding but trusts in the LORD with all his heart. Reason is good, and the Christian thinks rigorously; but he thinks as a creature under the Word, not as an autonomous judge above it. Whoever thinks he knows of himself knows nothing yet as he ought.

etymology: Greek philosopher of Stagira (384–322 B.C.), pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander; Greek Aristotelēs.
biblical_def: Aristotle was the Greek philosopher of the fourth century before Christ, pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander the Great, whose works on logic, ethics, physics, and metaphysics shaped the intellectual life of the West for two thousand years and entered deeply into the Christian schools through the medieval recovery of his texts. The dictionary regards Aristotle as a striking instance of common grace: a pagan who, by the light of nature that God gives to all men, reasoned with great power about the world, framed the logic the church would use to defend the faith, and discerned much that is true about virtue, causation, and order. Paul himself, on Mars’ hill, could quote the Greek poets and reason with the philosophers, for in God all men live and move and have their being. The truth Aristotle saw is God’s truth, however dimly grasped. Yet the dictionary marks the limits and the dangers. Aristotle did not know the God who made him; though the creation declared its Maker, the philosophers, knowing God, glorified Him not as God, and their foolish heart was darkened. And when his metaphysics was allowed to govern Christian theology rather than serve it—dictating what God must be apart from revelation—the servant overreached. The dictionary honors Aristotle’s common-grace gifts and uses his tools, while confessing that all the treasures of wisdom are hid in Christ, and the foolishness of God is wiser than men.
webster_summary: Greek philosopher (384–322 B.C.); an instance of common grace whose logic and insight the church uses, yet who knew not the true God, and whose metaphysics must serve, not govern, theology.

corruption_summary: Aristotle’s common-grace insight is honored, but he knew not the true God, and the danger is letting his metaphysics govern theology rather than serve it.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The matter to weigh is the right use of pagan wisdom. Aristotle saw much truth by the light of nature—common grace—and the church has rightly used his logic and learned from his observations; Paul himself reasoned with philosophers and quoted Greek poets. Yet two limits must be kept. First, Aristotle did not know the God who made him; though the creation declared its Maker, he, like the philosophers Paul describes, glorified Him not as God, and his heart was darkened. His system has no Trinity, no fall, no redemption. Second, the besetting danger of the schools was to let his metaphysics dictate what God must be, governing revelation instead of serving it.

The principle to recover is the right order of revelation over philosophy. All truth is God’s truth, and the believer may gather what is good from Aristotle as the Israelites carried gold out of Egypt; but the gold must be melted and reshaped under the Word, never set up as an idol. All the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hid in Christ, not in the Lyceum; the foolishness of God is wiser than men. Aristotle is a servant to be used, not a master to be obeyed.
